compare_blocks.body:
Align the conditions before reading: the same draft (a brand-manual introduction), the same client goal (a shop manager reads it and wants to sign up), the same quality problem (the second draft turned lyrical without settling whose voice it speaks in), the same five days left, and a budget for one more round. If one person is the client and the other only relays comments, or one took part in the original briefing, the difference in responsibilities or information may explain their choices.

Each row is written as a shared task with the basis each may attend to, and states which axis it illustrates. This pair shares S/N and T/F, so the discriminating rows fall on E/I and J/P, with one row marked as a shared axis where the two may look alike. Both types can take either approach; the table describes only which is taken up first more often.

| Shared task (fictional scenario) | ENFJ (Fe–Ni emphasis) | INFP (Fi–Ne emphasis) | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reading the second draft | May prefer to agree which parts of the draft are ready for revision | May keep several interpretations open until the same passages have been reviewed | J/P: form an arrangement that can move, or hold the judgement and keep reading |

compare_blocks.body:
Dealing with an outside writer, both may come across as easy to work with: perhaps two words of appreciation before the criticism, perhaps giving way when the other person starts defending. That impression comes more from the role (client or supplier), from previous collaborations and from the delivery pressure of the week than from shared letters.

The shared N and F describe emphasis in sourcing and judging: when gathering information, attending to patterns, connections and possibilities; when judging, putting people, values and context into the same consideration rather than settling for "make the changes and be done". The difference sits on the other two axes — whether attention and energy turn outward or inward (E/I), and whether outer life prefers forming arrangements or keeping options (J/P). Both axes describe emphasis, not ability, and not who is better at talking.

### When the second draft is still wrong, two trade-offs coexist

(Fictional scene.) The same brand-manual introduction comes back from the client with "still not right" after the second draft. One entry point organises the comments in an order the other person can take: say which passages are pointing the right way, attribute the problem to "the audience changed mid-way", and finish with three revisions, each with an example. The other entry point first brings the draft back to what it was supposed to be: this text is meant to speak for the shop managers, and every paragraph is currently talking about specifications.

The difference is not severity but what this round settles first. The first makes it easier for the other person to know what to do next, at the risk of polishing sentences while the intention stays put; the second is better at naming a directional problem, at the risk of leaving the writer without a sentence to start from. Both types can take either approach, and both can do both in one set of comments; which is more common depends on who knows the client better, who knows this kind of text better, and how much time is left in the round.

The criterion needs room: if this is the writer's first text of this kind and the budget covers one more round, both may break the comments down further; conversely, if goals were agreed earlier and the writer still has not followed them, both may state the problem more directly. Using "who is considered first" to separate the types gets both wrong.

### Why the four positions match in category and reverse in attitude

In the common four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Position for position: Feeling first, Intuition second, Sensing third, Thinking fourth; the categories match and the attitudes reverse. That correspondence is the model's description; it does not prescribe the order in which a person handles things and cannot assign anyone to a stage of the work.

The difference comes from two letters changing at once. E/I says whether the dominant process turns outward or inward: ENFJ's Fe turns outward and more often reads the expectations and relationships in the room first; INFP's Fi turns inward and more often calibrates its own values and responses first. J/P says whether the outward face prefers judging or perceiving: ENFJ more often forms an arrangement that can be pushed forward, INFP more often keeps options and keeps taking information in. A position is a position in the model, not a revision step and not a measure of character.

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the three passages below are the same kind of trade-off written in different settings, not a law of division. Who takes which part is arranged by the work, the experience with this kind of task and the time available; type does not enter the allocation.

### An outsourced draft going back and forth: the second version is still wrong

(Fictional scene.) A brand manual's introduction goes to an outside writer. The first draft reads like a product description, the second turns lyrical, and the client says "neither is what I want". Five days to deadline, budget for one more round.

One approach brings all three into a short call: let the client say in their own words who should read this and what they should do afterwards, put the writer's concerns on the table, and settle three revisions — open with a scene, give one person's name in the second paragraph, end with a single call to action. The other approach puts the two drafts and the original brief side by side and finds what the client was pointing at every time they said "no": not the tone but the stance — the manual speaks for the company, and the client wants it to speak for the shop managers.

Each has something missing: talking face to face easily turns a disagreement into a compromise that satisfies nobody in the third draft; comparing text alone may stay too abstract for the writer to know how to change a "stance". A workable combination is to write one sentence — whose voice this text speaks in — confirm it with the client, then break it into three concrete revisions with examples. Either person can do that step, depending on who knows the client and this kind of text better.

What counts is whether the third draft settles whose voice it speaks in, not whether the tone matches. The conditions have to be written too: if the writer has a record of late delivery, acceptance terms belong in a supplementary agreement; if the writer is new, revisions should go down to sentence-level examples. Neither response is about type; both are about delivery risk and the other person's experience.

A way to verify: attach an acceptance standard and one example to every must-change comment, then check next round what was actually solved and what remains. Tiers still work — must change, could improve, optional — but the tiers only order this round's workload, and do not show who cares more about the text or about delivery.

### A writer who keeps delivering late: replace or keep

(Fictional scene.) A writer the team has worked with for three months delivered three days late on each of the last two assignments, with no drop in quality. The project needs to scale up next month.

What can be compared are the shared conditions, not which type anyone resembles: whether the two delays had the same cause, whether they were flagged in advance, whether other collaborators were affected, what searching for and onboarding a replacement would cost, and how much error the scale-up period can absorb. One handling talks terms first — find out the cause, agree a schedule the writer can keep, and write down what happens if it recurs; the other costs out replacement first — assess how available candidates are and how long a handover takes, then decide whether to continue. Both types can choose either, and you can discuss revised terms while preparing a backup.

The disagreement is usually about the time scale: those who can wait will spend one more chance on quality, and those who are up against a launch would rather replace now. Writing those conditions down is more useful than arguing about who is more considerate.

### A younger cousin choosing a university major

(Fictional scene.) A younger cousin has the grades for a strong university and has applied for palaeontology; her family is worried about the choice. One entry point is to talk to her alone first: why this one, has she met anyone who studied it, and then how to raise it at home — what to say first, and who says it. The other entry point is to read the programme and where its graduates go, and work out whether she is drawn to studying fossils, working outdoors or something else about the field.

Each carries a risk: the one who plans the conversation easily turns "persuade the family" into the goal, and she ends up pushed into changing her application; the one who checks the field easily treats a genuine interest as a conclusion and ignores where she will be in four years. Which appears more often depends on who is present, who understands the field, and whether the family has already argued about it; the same person may take a different entry point in a different family.

A way to verify: let her write three lines herself — why I chose it, which course in it will be hardest, and what I do if I cannot transfer. She writes them, and only then does the conversation about changing happen. The point is that she checks it herself, rather than someone else judging her motive for her.

compare_blocks.body:
Reading INFP as "afraid to make demands" is the common error here. Introversion does not mean avoiding conflict, and it does not mean having no standards; the opinions may be very firm in writing, just not argued in the room.

Reading ENFJ as "only says nice things" is equally wrong. An extraverted Feeling preference does not mean abandoning standards; acceptance conditions may be raised very early, only framed inside the relationship.

The third misread is treating E/I as who is better at outward communication and J/P as who is better at planning. Both types may call a three-way meeting, and both may write first; the difference comes more often from duty, the other person's experience and time pressure. Judging by "who speaks first" or "who schedules first" gets both wrong.

sections.title: Quick answer

body: Dealing with an outside writer, both may come across as easy to work with: perhaps two words of appreciation before the criticism, perhaps giving way when the other person starts defending. That impression comes more from the role (client or supplier), from previous collaborations and from the delivery pressure of the week than from shared letters.

The shared N and F describe emphasis in sourcing and judging: when gathering information, attending to patterns, connections and possibilities; when judging, putting people, values and context into the same consideration rather than settling for "make the changes and be done". The difference sits on the other two axes — whether attention and energy turn outward or inward (E/I), and whether outer life prefers forming arrangements or keeping options (J/P). Both axes describe emphasis, not ability, and not who is better at talking.
### When the second draft is still wrong, two trade-offs coexist

(Fictional scene.) The same brand-manual introduction comes back from the client with "still not right" after the second draft. One entry point organises the comments in an order the other person can take: say which passages are pointing the right way, attribute the problem to "the audience changed mid-way", and finish with three revisions, each with an example. The other entry point first brings the draft back to what it was supposed to be: this text is meant to speak for the shop managers, and every paragraph is currently talking about specifications.

The difference is not severity but what this round settles first. The first makes it easier for the other person to know what to do next, at the risk of polishing sentences while the intention stays put; the second is better at naming a directional problem, at the risk of leaving the writer without a sentence to start from. Both types can take either approach, and both can do both in one set of comments; which is more common depends on who knows the client better, who knows this kind of text better, and how much time is left in the round.

The criterion needs room: if this is the writer's first text of this kind and the budget covers one more round, both may break the comments down further; conversely, if goals were agreed earlier and the writer still has not followed them, both may state the problem more directly. Using "who is considered first" to separate the types gets both wrong.
### Why the four positions match in category and reverse in attitude

In the common four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Position for position: Feeling first, Intuition second, Sensing third, Thinking fourth; the categories match and the attitudes reverse. That correspondence is the model's description; it does not prescribe the order in which a person handles things and cannot assign anyone to a stage of the work.

The difference comes from two letters changing at once. E/I says whether the dominant process turns outward or inward: ENFJ's Fe turns outward and more often reads the expectations and relationships in the room first; INFP's Fi turns inward and more often calibrates its own values and responses first. J/P says whether the outward face prefers judging or perceiving: ENFJ more often forms an arrangement that can be pushed forward, INFP more often keeps options and keeps taking information in. A position is a position in the model, not a revision step and not a measure of character.

The attitude labelling of the third process (Se and Si) varies between sources; this page lists the common writing, so check the conventions of any table that differs. Base descriptions are in the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

body: Scope note: the three passages below are the same kind of trade-off written in different settings, not a law of division. Who takes which part is arranged by the work, the experience with this kind of task and the time available; type does not enter the allocation.
### An outsourced draft going back and forth: the second version is still wrong

(Fictional scene.) A brand manual's introduction goes to an outside writer. The first draft reads like a product description, the second turns lyrical, and the client says "neither is what I want". Five days to deadline, budget for one more round.

One approach brings all three into a short call: let the client say in their own words who should read this and what they should do afterwards, put the writer's concerns on the table, and settle three revisions — open with a scene, give one person's name in the second paragraph, end with a single call to action. The other approach puts the two drafts and the original brief side by side and finds what the client was pointing at every time they said "no": not the tone but the stance — the manual speaks for the company, and the client wants it to speak for the shop managers.

Each has something missing: talking face to face easily turns a disagreement into a compromise that satisfies nobody in the third draft; comparing text alone may stay too abstract for the writer to know how to change a "stance". A workable combination is to write one sentence — whose voice this text speaks in — confirm it with the client, then break it into three concrete revisions with examples. Either person can do that step, depending on who knows the client and this kind of text better.

What counts is whether the third draft settles whose voice it speaks in, not whether the tone matches. The conditions have to be written too: if the writer has a record of late delivery, acceptance terms belong in a supplementary agreement; if the writer is new, revisions should go down to sentence-level examples. Neither response is about type; both are about delivery risk and the other person's experience.

A way to verify: attach an acceptance standard and one example to every must-change comment, then check next round what was actually solved and what remains. Tiers still work — must change, could improve, optional — but the tiers only order this round's workload, and do not show who cares more about the text or about delivery.
### A writer who keeps delivering late: replace or keep
(Fictional scene.) A writer the team has worked with for three months delivered three days late on each of the last two assignments, with no drop in quality. The project needs to scale up next month.

What can be compared are the shared conditions, not which type anyone resembles: whether the two delays had the same cause, whether they were flagged in advance, whether other collaborators were affected, what searching for and onboarding a replacement would cost, and how much error the scale-up period can absorb. One handling talks terms first — find out the cause, agree a schedule the writer can keep, and write down what happens if it recurs; the other costs out replacement first — assess how available candidates are and how long a handover takes, then decide whether to continue. Both types can choose either, and you can discuss revised terms while preparing a backup.

The disagreement is usually about the time scale: those who can wait will spend one more chance on quality, and those who are up against a launch would rather replace now. Writing those conditions down is more useful than arguing about who is more considerate.
### A younger cousin choosing a university major

(Fictional scene.) A younger cousin has the grades for a strong university and has applied for palaeontology; her family is worried about the choice. One entry point is to talk to her alone first: why this one, has she met anyone who studied it, and then how to raise it at home — what to say first, and who says it. The other entry point is to read the programme and where its graduates go, and work out whether she is drawn to studying fossils, working outdoors or something else about the field.

Each carries a risk: the one who plans the conversation easily turns "persuade the family" into the goal, and she ends up pushed into changing her application; the one who checks the field easily treats a genuine interest as a conclusion and ignores where she will be in four years. Which appears more often depends on who is present, who understands the field, and whether the family has already argued about it; the same person may take a different entry point in a different family.

A way to verify: let her write three lines herself — why I chose it, which course in it will be hardest, and what I do if I cannot transfer. She writes them, and only then does the conversation about changing happen. The point is that she checks it herself, rather than someone else judging her motive for her.

body: Reading INFP as "afraid to make demands" is the common error here. Introversion does not mean avoiding conflict, and it does not mean having no standards; the opinions may be very firm in writing, just not argued in the room.

Reading ENFJ as "only says nice things" is equally wrong. An extraverted Feeling preference does not mean abandoning standards; acceptance conditions may be raised very early, only framed inside the relationship.

The third misread is treating E/I as who is better at outward communication and J/P as who is better at planning. Both types may call a three-way meeting, and both may write first; the difference comes more often from duty, the other person's experience and time pressure. Judging by "who speaks first" or "who schedules first" gets both wrong.

The other entry point first brings the draft back to what it was supposed to be: this text is meant to speak for the shop managers, and every paragraph is currently talking about specifications.

The difference is not severity but what this round settles first. The first makes it easier for the other person to know what to do next, at the risk of polishing sentences while the intention stays put; the second is better at naming a directional problem, at the risk of leaving the writer without a sentence to start from. Both types can take either approach, and both can do both in one set of comments; which is more common depends on who knows the client better, who knows this kind of text better, and how much time is left in the round.

The criterion needs room: if this is the writer's first text of this kind and the budget covers one more round, both may break the comments down further; conversely, if goals were agreed earlier and the writer still has not followed them, both may state the problem more directly. Using "who is considered first" to separate the types gets both wrong.

### Why the four positions match in category and reverse in attitude

In the common four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Position for position: Feeling first, Intuition second, Sensing third, Thinking fourth; the categories match and the attitudes reverse. That correspondence is the model's description; it does not prescribe the order in which a person handles things and cannot assign anyone to a stage of the work.

The difference comes from two letters changing at once. E/I says whether the dominant process turns outward or inward: ENFJ's Fe turns outward and more often reads the expectations and relationships in the room first; INFP's Fi turns inward and more often calibrates its own values and responses first. J/P says whether the outward face prefers judging or perceiving: ENFJ more often forms an arrangement that can be pushed forward, INFP more often keeps options and keeps taking information in. A position is a position in the model, not a revision step and not a measure of character.

The attitude labelling of the third process (Se and Si) varies between sources; this page lists the common writing, so check the conventions of any table that differs. Base descriptions are in the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions before reading: the same draft (a brand-manual introduction), the same client goal (a shop manager reads it and wants to sign up), the same quality problem (the second draft turned lyrical without settling whose voice it speaks in), the same five days left, and a budget for one more round. If one person is the client and the other only relays comments, or one took part in the original briefing, the difference in responsibilities or information may explain their choices.

Each row is written as a shared task with the basis each may attend to, and states which axis it illustrates. This pair shares S/N and T/F, so the discriminating rows fall on E/I and J/P, with one row marked as a shared axis where the two may look alike. Both types can take either approach; the table describes only which is taken up first more often.

| Shared task (fictional scenario) | ENFJ (Fe–Ni emphasis) | INFP (Fi–Ne emphasis) | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reading the second draft | May prefer to agree which parts of the draft are ready for revision | May keep several interpretations open until the same passages have been reviewed | J/P: form an arrangement that can move, or hold the judgement and keep reading |
| Writing comments | May agree on a provisional list of revision steps with examples | May leave several revision options open for discussion | J/P: give a conclusion outward, or leave room for discussion |
| The other person defends on the spot | May find discussion helps clarify what the disagreement means | May find private reflection helps clarify the same disagreement | E/I: energy placed in the exchange, or sorted internally first |
| Whether to hold a three-way call | May clarify the shared goal by talking it through with the group | May clarify the same goal by thinking it through privately | E/I: outward interaction, or internal sorting before going outward |
| Setting the scope and deadline for this round | May agree on a provisional deadline within the shared constraints | May keep more than one feasible deadline open until the scope is clearer | J/P: form an arrangement, or keep room to adjust |
| Final check | May confirm the other person is still willing to take another round | May confirm the draft still reflects its original intention | N and F (shared): both may look at the relationship and the intention |
sections.title: ENFJ and INFP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: the three passages below are the same kind of trade-off written in different settings, not a law of division. Who takes which part is arranged by the work, the experience with this kind of task and the time available; type does not enter the allocation.

### An outsourced draft going back and forth: the second version is still wrong

(Fictional scene.) A brand manual's introduction goes to an outside writer. The first draft reads like a product description, the second turns lyrical, and the client says "neither is what I want". Five days to deadline, budget for one more round.

One approach brings all three into a short call: let the client say in their own words who should read this and what they should do afterwards, put the writer's concerns on the table, and settle three revisions — open with a scene, give one person's name in the second paragraph, end with a single call to action. The other approach puts the two drafts and the original brief side by side and finds what the client was pointing at every time they said "no": not the tone but the stance — the manual speaks for the company, and the client wants it to speak for the shop managers.

Each has something missing: talking face to face easily turns a disagreement into a compromise that satisfies nobody in the third draft; comparing text alone may stay too abstract for the writer to know how to change a "stance". A workable combination is to write one sentence — whose voice this text speaks in — confirm it with the client, then break it into three concrete revisions with examples. Either person can do that step, depending on who knows the client and this kind of text better.

What counts is whether the third draft settles whose voice it speaks in, not whether the tone matches. The conditions have to be written too: if the writer has a record of late delivery, acceptance terms belong in a supplementary agreement; if the writer is new, revisions should go down to sentence-level examples. Neither response is about type; both are about delivery risk and the other person's experience.

A way to verify: attach an acceptance standard and one example to every must-change comment, then check next round what was actually solved and what remains. Tiers still work — must change, could improve, optional — but the tiers only order this round's workload, and do not show who cares more about the text or about delivery.

### A writer who keeps delivering late: replace or keep

(Fictional scene.) A writer the team has worked with for three months delivered three days late on each of the last two assignments, with no drop in quality. The project needs to scale up next month.

What can be compared are the shared conditions, not which type anyone resembles: whether the two delays had the same cause, whether they were flagged in advance, whether other collaborators were affected, what searching for and onboarding a replacement would cost, and how much error the scale-up period can absorb. One handling talks terms first — find out the cause, agree a schedule the writer can keep, and write down what happens if it recurs; the other costs out replacement first — assess how available candidates are and how long a handover takes, then decide whether to continue. Both types can choose either, and you can discuss revised terms while preparing a backup.

The disagreement is usually about the time scale: those who can wait will spend one more chance on quality, and those who are up against a launch would rather replace now. Writing those conditions down is more useful than arguing about who is more considerate.

### A younger cousin choosing a university major

(Fictional scene.) A younger cousin has the grades for a strong university and has applied for palaeontology; her family is worried about the choice. One entry point is to talk to her alone first: why this one, has she met anyone who studied it, and then how to raise it at home — what to say first, and who says it. The other entry point is to read the programme and where its graduates go, and work out whether she is drawn to studying fossils, working outdoors or something else about the field.

Each carries a risk: the one who plans the conversation easily turns "persuade the family" into the goal, and she ends up pushed into changing her application; the one who checks the field easily treats a genuine interest as a conclusion and ignores where she will be in four years. Which appears more often depends on who is present, who understands the field, and whether the family has already argued about it; the same person may take a different entry point in a different family.

A way to verify: let her write three lines herself — why I chose it, which course in it will be hardest, and what I do if I cannot transfer. She writes them, and only then does the conversation about changing happen. The point is that she checks it herself, rather than someone else judging her motive for her.
sections.title: ENFJ and INFP at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
Reading INFP as "afraid to make demands" is the common error here. Introversion does not mean avoiding conflict, and it does not mean having no standards; the opinions may be very firm in writing, just not argued in the room.

Reading ENFJ as "only says nice things" is equally wrong. An extraverted Feeling preference does not mean abandoning standards; acceptance conditions may be raised very early, only framed inside the relationship.

The third misread is treating E/I as who is better at outward communication and J/P as who is better at planning. Both types may call a three-way meeting, and both may write first; the difference comes more often from duty, the other person's experience and time pressure. Judging by "who speaks first" or "who schedules first" gets both wrong.
sections.title: ENFJ and INFP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check whether the item bank, version and answering language were the same, then look at the situation you answered from: were you the one making demands or the one receiving them, was there delivery pressure, which experience were you referring to. Role rewrites answers, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

The practice is to review several comparable situations rather than catch one reaction: take three recent occasions when you wrote revision comments and note three lines for each — your role and constraints, whether you handled the goal of the text or its executability first, and why you made that trade-off. If one kind of reason recurs, it is worth discussing as your emphasis; it is not a rule for typing, and it does not require counting sentence order or frequency.
sections.title: ENFJ and INFP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Anyone hearing that sentence more often thinks first about what is wrong, how far it has to change, and how much time is left this round — true for both types; what comes to mind first depends more on whether the goal was stated clearly, on the other person's experience, and on who said it.

With the same draft and feedback, one person may find it easier to clarify the brief in conversation. Another may prefer to reread the draft privately before discussing it. Either can then ask for a specific example, explain what needs to change and agree on the next step. The order of those actions cannot establish a type.
items.question: Does "needs more work" mean the same thing to ENFJ and INFP?

items.answer:
In the common four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. The categories correspond position by position and every name differs, because the attitude in each slot reverses.

E/I changes the direction of the dominant process, and J/P changes whether the outward face prefers judging or perceiving. The attitude labelling of the third process varies between sources; this page lists the common version, so check the conventions of a table that differs. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and cannot be used to infer the order of work.
items.question: Why are all four function names different for ENFJ and INFP?

items.answer:
Yes, but not on "who considers people more". A preference describes which basis is taken up first more often, not whether the capacity exists. If the other person has a record of late delivery, ENFJ may also put acceptance terms into a supplementary agreement; if the other person is new, INFP may also break the comments into sentence-level examples.

What discriminates better is reviewing several comparable situations: do you care more about whether this requirement can be applied consistently and whether the other person can execute it, or about whether this text has turned into something else. The tone of one exchange cannot establish a type.
items.question: INFP can also manage a supplier's feelings and ENFJ can also be blunt — can they still be told apart?

items.answer:
Both can do it; the difference is experience and available time, not type. Content acceptance can be split into setting the standard, reading the draft, writing comments and negotiating the revision; the same person is usually more practised in some of those than others, and that can change with the project.

The steadier basis for division is the record of work, experience with this kind of text, and how much time is available in this period. A fictional revision sheet makes a good exercise: write "the problem with the intention" and "three revisions with examples" separately, and see which was easier to put into concrete terms. That is self-observation, not an ability rating, and it does not point to a type.
items.question: Who is better at managing suppliers or accepting content?

items.answer:
One possible disagreement is how hard the comments should land: one worries that too soft means the work will not be done, the other worries that too hard means the writer will only copy the wording. That disagreement can follow from who is responsible for delivery, what the writer needs and how much time is left.

A workable agreement is two lines per comment: one saying what is wrong with the draft, one saying how you want it changed. Written separately, neither has to guess for the other; if the two disagree, go back to the client's original brief rather than arguing about whose reading is more accurate.
items.question: Where do ENFJ and INFP most often get stuck on a content project?

items.answer:
Start by checking whether both results came from the same questionnaire and language version. If it reports scores and explains a boundary, check the reported E/I and J/P scores against that guidance. A changed label alone cannot explain the difference.

If scores sit on the line, reviewing the situation you answered from is more useful than retesting in another role — were you making demands or receiving them, was there delivery pressure. If you retest, keep the item bank, language version and conditions as comparable as possible, and record each result with its situation; a single difference does not establish a tendency.
